import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1102

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1102](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1102)
-/
open Squarefree Set Order Filter Topology
namespace Erdos1102

/--
Property P : A set $A ⊆ ℕ $ has property P, if for all $n ≥ 1$ the set
$ \{a ∈ A | n + a\text{ is squarefree}\}$ is finite.
-/
def HasPropertyP (A : Set ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ n ≥ 1, {a ∈ A | Squarefree (n + a)}.Finite

/--
Property Q : A set $A ⊆ ℕ $ has property Q, if the set
$\{n ∈ ℕ  | ∀ a ∈ A, n > a\text{ implies }n + a\text{ is squarefree}\}$ is infinite.
-/
def HasPropertyQ (A : Set ℕ) : Prop :=
  {n : ℕ | ∀ a ∈ A, a < n → Squarefree (n + a)}.Infinite

/--
If `A = {a₁ < a₂ < …}` has property P,
then `A` has natural density `0`.
Equivalently, `(a_j / j) → ∞` as `j → ∞`.
--/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/1e075c4f6e8a907b924647fa88238f978e941742/ErdosProblem1102PropertyP.lean"]
theorem erdos_1102.density_zero_of_P
    (A : ℕ → ℕ)
    (h_inc : StrictMono A)
    (hP : HasPropertyP (range A)) :
    Tendsto (fun j => (A j / j : ℝ)) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

/--
Conversely, for any function `f : ℕ → ℕ` that goes to infinity,
there exists a strictly increasing sequence `A = {a₁ < a₂ < …}`
with property P such that `(a_j / j) ≤ f(j)` for all `j`.
--/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/1e075c4f6e8a907b924647fa88238f978e941742/ErdosProblem1102PropertyP.lean"]
theorem erdos_1102.exists_sequence_with_P
    (f : ℕ → ℕ) (h_inf : Tendsto f atTop atTop)
    (h_pos : ∀ n, f n ≠ 0) :
    ∃ A : ℕ → ℕ, StrictMono A ∧
    HasPropertyP (range A) ∧
    ∀ j : ℕ, (A j : ℝ) / j ≤ f j := by
  sorry

/--
Every sequence with property Q has upper density at most `6 / π^2`.
--/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/1e075c4f6e8a907b924647fa88238f978e941742/ErdosProblem1102PropertyQDensity.lean"]
theorem erdos_1102.upper_density_Q
    (A : ℕ → ℕ) (h_inc : StrictMono A)
    (hQ : HasPropertyQ (range A)) :
    limsup (fun j : ℕ  ↦ (j / A j : ℝ)) atTop ≤ 6 / Real.pi^2 := by
  sorry

/--
There exists an infinite sequence $A = {a₁ < a₂ < …} ⊂ \mathsf{SF}$ where
$\mathsf{SF} := \mathbb{N} \setminus \bigcup_{p} p^{2}\mathbb{N}$, i.e. the set of
squarefree numbers. The set `A` has property `Q` and natural density `6 / π^2`.
Equivalently, `(j / a_j) → 6/π^2` as `j → ∞`.
--/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/1e075c4f6e8a907b924647fa88238f978e941742/ErdosProblem1102PropertyQDensity.lean"]
theorem erdos_1102.lower_density_Q_exists :
    ∃ A : ℕ → ℕ, StrictMono A ∧
    (∀ j, Squarefree (A j)) ∧
    HasPropertyQ (range A) ∧
    Tendsto (fun j : ℕ  ↦ (j / A j : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 (6 / Real.pi^2)) := by
  sorry

end Erdos1102

findings.description: The docstring at lines 56–58 says the result holds for any `f : ℕ → ℕ` tending to infinity, but omits the positive-valued hypothesis `h_pos : ∀ n, f n ≠ 0` present in the Lean statement. That hypothesis matters: let f(1)=0 and f(n)=n+1 otherwise. This function tends to infinity, but the bound at j=1 would force A(1)≤0, whereas strict monotonicity implies A(1)≥1. This counterexample was proved independently in Lean. The formal theorem itself correctly includes the hypothesis and matches the source.
findings.source_evidence: Van Doorn–Tao, arXiv:2512.01087v2, Theorem 1(ii), states the pointwise bound a_j/j≤f(j) in the positive-integer convention; its construction begins with a_j=j. The cited ErdosProblem1102PropertyP.lean at commit 1e075c4f6e8a907b924647fa88238f978e941742 explicitly includes `(h_pos : ∀ n, f n ≠ 0)` in its corresponding theorem: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Woett/Lean-files/1e075c4f6e8a907b924647fa88238f978e941742/ErdosProblem1102PropertyP.lean.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to say “for any positive-valued function `f : ℕ → ℕ` that goes to infinity.” No change to the Lean statement is needed.

reformulations.difference: The paper uses a positive-indexed sequence of positive integers; Lean uses `A : ℕ → ℕ`, allows A(0)=0, and requires the bound at every natural index.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a fixed bound f, restricting a Lean witness to positive indices gives positive values because StrictMono A implies A(j)≥j. Removing A(0) preserves property P. Conversely, extend a positive-indexed positive-valued sequence by A(0)=0. This preserves strict increase and P, since P is unchanged by finite modifications; the new j=0 inequality is automatically true because real division by zero gives zero. The equivalence between these two existential formulations was proved in Lean. The source's positive-valued f is represented by h_pos, with its otherwise irrelevant value at zero chosen positive.

reformulations.difference: Lean expresses upper density as `limsup (fun j => (j / A j : ℝ)) atTop`, rather than a limsup of counting proportions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a strictly increasing enumeration, the number of range elements strictly below A(j) is exactly j; this identity was proved in Lean. Inclusive counting at A(j) differs by at most one, contributing at most 1/A(j), which tends to zero. Between successive sequence elements the inclusive counting function is constant, so the counting proportion is largest at the left endpoint. Consequently its limsup equals limsup j/A(j). Strict monotonicity also gives A(j)≥j, hence 0≤j/A(j)≤1; Lean proofs checked the boundedness and coboundedness needed for the real-valued limsup. The full limsup equality was checked mathematically, not proved in the scratch file.

reformulations.difference: The paper's equivalent sequence formulation is a_j/j→π²/6; Lean instead states j/A(j)→6/π².
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Both limiting constants are nonzero, and inversion is continuous at each. Taking reciprocals therefore converts either limit into the other. The identity (A(j)/j)⁻¹=j/A(j) also holds under Lean's totalized division, so the zero-index term causes no difficulty. This reciprocal-limit equivalence was proved independently in Lean.
